stories.headline: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons
stories.script: Our lead story today. A group of countries headed by Russia and the United States is working to stop talks on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, the Guardian reports. They plan to use a United Nations conference this month to block the proposals. Many see the meeting as a turning point after years of debate over how to govern weapons systems run by artificial intelligence. Efforts to close that gap in oversight now appear to be at risk. How strong the opposition is should become clear at a diplomatic retreat beginning on Friday. The retreat comes ahead of the seventh review conference on certain conventional weapons, which 128 countries are expected to attend in Geneva from 16 to 20 November.
stories.whyThisMatters: A group of countries headed by Russia and the United States is working to stop talks on legally binding rules for autonomous weapons, the Guardian reports.
keyPoints: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons

stories.headline: Google sued over suicide-related AI chats on school computer
stories.script: Turning to the United States. A 13-year-old girl's parents are suing Google, The Economic Times reports. They allege that she used the company's AI technology on a computer her school gave her to plan a possible suicide and her own funeral. Companies building AI in the United States face a growing number of similar lawsuits. OpenAI is defending several wrongful death claims, including one brought by Adam Raine's parents. The 16-year-old allegedly took his own life using methods suggested by ChatGPT.
stories.whyThisMatters: A 13-year-old girl's parents are suing Google, The Economic Times reports.
keyPoints: Google sued over suicide-related AI chats on school computer

stories.headline: Nigel Farage's exit from the Telegraph may be cause for cheer. But there’s a sobering side to this story | Jane Martinson
stories.script: Around the world. Writing in the Guardian, Jane Martinson argues that Nigel Farage's departure from the Daily Telegraph has a more troubling side. In her view, the shake-up at the paper seems driven more by a move toward artificial intelligence than by politics, and journalism will bear the cost. Farage has written columns for the Telegraph since 2016. Most of them promoted the party he leads, first the Brexit party and now Reform UK, or accused his opponents of being weak on immigration. The paper, which is short of money, paid him roughly £4,000 a month, close to half a million pounds over the past ten years. This week it emerged that the Telegraph's new German owners, Axel Springer, no longer want his columns. People close to Farage, however, say he quit.

stories.headline: VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding
stories.script: From the research desk. In a paper titled VFlash: Fast, Accurate Visual Planning via Flash Primitive Decoding, the researchers take on a speed problem in AI systems used for robotics and self-driving cars. These systems do not have to plan only in words. They can also plan visually, using points, boxes drawn around objects, and paths to mark their goals and predict movement. But current models that combine vision and language build these plans one coordinate at a time, so more detailed plans take longer to produce. VFlash takes advantage of the predictable shape of these visual elements to work out all of their coordinates at once. It relies on a small helper model that drafts an entire element in a single step.
